extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and evaluative principles for discovering and playing the 'game' or pattern in an improvised scene (includes Sandy Carroll variants, pattern/repetition tools, timing, and teaching notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandy Carroll (control) technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Play a character who takes control and makes offers that the partner accepts, often making the partner feel 'cleverer than the game' and producing rewarding results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Sandy Carroll to learn playing with audience members and to make partners look good. Make offers that invite a 'yes' but create difficulty/suffering for the receiver (e.g., arch/sarcastic acceptance like 'Sounds good to me!'). Practice in front of the group and side-coach; this counters the tendency to seek reaction and helps improvisers play scenes with audience members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Sandy Carroll (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A restricted Sandy Carroll who answers only with 'No', 'Why should I?', 'Fuck off', 'I'd rather die'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use: Negative Sandy Carroll generates massive conflict quickly but typically blocks and cancels everything, preventing development. The real lesson of the exercise is 'don't do this.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet Sandy Carroll (accept-without-adding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A player accepts their partner's offers and lets the partner take the lead, saying yes but stopping short of adding anything new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play in pairs first; Diet Sandy Carroll is useful for Quiets and for training Clevers to connect to partner offers. Example mother-daughter scene shows Diet Sandy Carroll allowing the other player to drive the scene while still adding small details but not developing the partner's ideas. It teaches acceptance without taking over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret Diet Sandy Carroll (hidden-collusion exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two players privately decide which will be Diet Sandy Carroll; the Diet player fearlessly accepts but refrains from making offers while the other makes minimal offers to keep the story moving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: prevent 'yes-and' failure and encourage developing partner's ideas. Important procedural notes: set who starts and who speaks first to hedge bets; play on stage (not privately) so the audience tries to divine identities; a single early offer may give the game away but the focus is the players' states. Example: the school playground bully/sweets mime demonstrates exemplary acceptance. This exercise builds the habit of developing partner ideas and stitches scenes together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make offers to which a 'yes' creates suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft offers so that accepting them (a 'yes') produces some kind of trouble or complication for the accepting character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This increases conflict and interest in a scene. Practice making such offers in exercises and coach players to spot how a simple acceptance can lead to situations that challenge characters (example: being fired but reacting happily creates comic tension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes And — thoughtful, subtle, detailed acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Yes And' not merely as an ecstatic or euphoriac affirmation but as a thoughtful, subtle, and convincing way to accept and build on offers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This version of Yes And is less euphoric but provides greater scope and substance. Encourage acceptances that are detailed and that tie back to partner offers rather than simply escalating for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach 'Finding the Game' to experienced improvisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve formal teaching of 'Finding The Game' until improvisers are more experienced, often after a few public performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: Finding The Game is easy (and therefore seductive) but limiting; presenting it too early may tempt beginners to substitute it for the harder work of storytelling. Teachers should avoid mystifying the technique and instead introduce it when students have sufficient stage experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding the game = identifying a repeating pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'game' in a scene is typically a pattern you can repeat; finding the game often involves identifying something you can repeat and exploit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to mystical accounts, there is no required 'game move' to spot; simply decide what to repeat. The game is often discoverable early (often cited as within the first three lines) but what matters is the recognisable repetition that structures the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition and the rule of three for anticipation and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (including the rule of three) creates audience expectation; violating or surprising that expectation on the third iteration can produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create effective surprise, establish X at least twice before breaking it with Y; examples and children's stories illustrate how repetition builds expectation and allows a third iteration to be a comic reversal. The rule of three is an efficient instantiation of this general principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate repetition, reincorporation, and callbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand three distinct uses of repetition: repeating within a scene to form a game; callbacks (repetition across scenes as an external joke); and reincorporation (narrative return that provides point within the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callbacks are external and bond the audience (in-joke); reincorporation exists inside the scene's narrative world and adds structure/point. Reincorporation helps provide 'point' and may be funny; callbacks are primarily funny and may not contribute to narrative point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a calm platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin scenes with a calm, clear platform to give performers somewhere to go and to allow for escalation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A calm platform makes raising the stakes and heightening easier and gives the scene an accessible baseline from which to accelerate or change tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening / raising the stakes to prolong interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Use heightening (going up the absurdity curve) and raising stakes to accelerate energy and keep scenes engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: progressively increasing agitation in a doctor/patient scene or adding increasingly bizarre charges in a sketch. Heightening helps prolong interest but must be used judiciously—sketch writers often design accelerating structures that improvised scenes may struggle to match.

rubrics_metrics.name: End the scene when the audience knows the 'point'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the audience fully understands the point of the scene (the change, suffering, or resolution), it is likely time to end it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques for ending: violate an established pattern, use reincorporation, canceling, or complete a routine. Be aware that once 'point' is clear, continued repetition may diminish impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns can be actions as well as words
rubrics_metrics.description: A scenic pattern need not be literal repetition of lines; it can be repetition of actions or behaviors (e.g., repeatedly 'suspecting different diseases').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use action-based patterns to create characters (e.g., hypochondriac) or to structure a scene without verbatim repetition. This broadens the ways a game can be discovered and played.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher procedural setup to shape audience perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Directorial choices—such as deciding who starts on stage and who speaks first—affect how the audience reads roles (e.g., who appears 'free' vs 'Diet Sandy Carroll').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these setup choices to hedge bets and increase the effectiveness of exercises like Secret Diet Sandy Carroll. The instructor's framing is an important tool for practice and for the audience's interpretive work.
